d.title: Three reasons, and all three are structural rather than about capability
d.caption: Note what none of them says: that specialists are better at their domain. **All three are about permissions, a context budget or ownership** — facts about the system's boundaries, not about how well a model performs. Which is what makes them checkable: you can say whether two tool sets need different permissions, and you cannot say whether three agents are “better at their jobs”.

items.label: Different permissions
items.desc: An agent that can issue refunds and one that reads docs should not be one agent with both tools.

items.label: Context that will not fit or should not mix
items.desc: Twenty tools per turn is a large fixed cost, and untrusted descriptions should not sit beside privileged tools.

items.label: Separate ownership and release cycles
items.desc: A team boundary — an interface is worth its cost when two groups evolve separately.

d.title: Three reasons that sound structural and are not
d.caption: **An org chart solves human communication-bandwidth and accountability problems, and neither constraint applies here** — so copying the structure imports the coordination cost without the reason for it. *“Each agent is simpler”* is true of each agent and false of the system. And *“it will scale better”* has a measurement against it: **more model calls per request is the opposite of scaling — 5 against 3 for the same answer.**

nodes.label: 'It mirrors how a human team works'
'Each agent is simpler'
nodes.sub: true of each, false of the system

nodes.label: More calls per request is not scaling

d.title: Four things are added, and no individual agent owns any of them
d.caption: Splitting one agent into three genuinely does reduce each one's prompt and tool list. **What it adds — handoff logic, the shared state's contract, attribution, the coordination failures — belongs to the system rather than to any agent, so each agent can be correct while the system fails.** And the sharper point is that the complexity became **harder to see**: a complicated agent is complicated in a file you can read.

nodes.label: Owned by the system, not an agent
And harder to see than a long file

d.title: Not whether several agents could work, but whether one cannot
d.caption: **Multiple agents will usually work; so will one, more cheaply and with fewer gaps** — which is 11.1's ladder reasoning one level up. The asymmetry holds too, and it is the practical argument: **splitting later is additive, while merging later means discovering which boundaries were load-bearing, and that needs measurements nobody took** while the system was still three agents.

nodes.label: One agent with the tools it needs
And that needs measurements nobody took
nodes.sub: so the default is cheap insurance

d.title: One list, so every worker's output is in every later worker's prompt
d.caption: The shared list is the simplest channel and it has a price: **context for free, and tokens paid for repeatedly** — 12.7's trade. Which is also why `name` earns its place: **without it a later worker sees a sequence of `AIMessage`s with no attribution and cannot tell which agent said what, and 12.8's blame problem is unanswerable.** The field looks cosmetic and is the only thing making the list readable.

d.title: A router draws once; a supervisor draws once per turn
d.caption: Same failure as 11.2's — a routing key not in the path map — but the exposure is different: **a router classifies once per request, so an unmapped category is one draw; a supervisor classifies once per turn, so a five-turn task is five draws from the same distribution.** Which means **a supervisor needs the default branch more than a router does**, and for the same reason: the set of strings a model can emit is not enumerable.

d.title: A supervisor that never says FINISH, stopped by a turn budget
d.caption: The alternation runs four times and then the graph **returns a usable answer** rather than raising. **So a supervisor needs all of 11.8's guards — a turn budget, a give-up node and a default branch — and needs them more than a single agent does, because it has one more thing that can fail: the coordination decision itself.** That is a failure mode a single agent does not have at all.

d.title: A decision point between every pair of steps, and what belongs in it
d.caption: Not specialisation — a prompt does that for one model call instead of two. **What a supervisor adds is a place to put policy**, and these four are what that place is for. **If there is no policy, the extra turn is a model call that decides who works next — and a router would have decided that once, for free.** 12.3's swarm makes it concrete by removing the turn, and with it the only place these could live.

nodes.label: Permission checks
nodes.sub: may this worker run for this user?

nodes.label: Approval gates (9.8)
nodes.sub: pause before the worker that acts

nodes.label: Observability
nodes.sub: one place knows the whole plan

nodes.label: No policy? Then it is a call to pick a worker
nodes.sub: a router did that once, free

d.title: The reason travelled with the destination
d.caption: `Command(goto=target, update={...})` is 8.8's case exactly: **the handoff carries both where to go and why, in one return value**, so nothing has to reconstruct the reason from state afterwards. And the count is the swarm's real advantage — **no supervisor means no coordination turn, so one model call per step rather than two.**

d.title: Two correct agents, and a loop that is a property of the pair
d.caption: Each one correctly declines a request outside its area. **There is no bug in either agent's logic, no wrong prompt and no malfunction — and reviewing either one in isolation would find nothing.** Which is 12.1's point made concrete: the complexity moved into the handoffs, and this failure lives entirely in the gap between two correct components, where no code review is looking.

nodes.label: The loop belongs to the pair

d.title: The counter cannot be per-agent, so it lives in the state
d.caption: **No single agent knows how many hops have happened — one counting its own handoffs cannot see the other's — so the counter has to be in the shared state, which every agent increments and every agent reads.** And the escalation is the swarm's give-up node (11.3): without it, exhausting the budget is an exception rather than an answer. Escalating to a human is also the **right** outcome here: two agents that cannot place a request is exactly what a person should see.

nodes.label: An agent counts its own handoffs
So: hops in the shared state
Without it: an exception, not an answer
And a human is the right recipient

d.title: State crosses by key name, which is right for messages and wrong for notes
d.caption: 10.1's rule unchanged, with sharper consequences at a team boundary: **a team with a `candidates` key the top level also declares has its working notes merged upward, and a team whose key the parent does not declare has its update silently discarded.** So the boundary is a **schema design** decision — and across a team boundary the wrapper with an explicit mapping is the better of the two, because then the interface is code a rename breaks visibly.

nodes.label: So: name internal keys so they cannot collide
Or wrap with an explicit mapping

d.title: Five top-level checkpoints, and the team's turns arrived in one of them
d.caption: `get_state(cfg, subgraphs=True)` reaches inside, but **the default is opacity — and what is opaque here is an agent's decisions: which worker the team's supervisor chose, and why.** That is precisely the information you want when the output is wrong, and 12.8's blame problem is already hard without a layer of the reasoning invisible by default. **So a hierarchy makes the hardest multi-agent failure harder.**

d.title: Two coordination calls per level, before any work happens
d.caption: Simple and unforgiving arithmetic on a task that needs **one** worker turn. **Each level adds a coordination model call per unit of work, a state boundary to get right, and a layer of opacity in the parent's trace** — and only the first of those three shows up in a bill. The other two show up when something is wrong, which is why the depth decision is not purely a cost question.

d.title: One level, and only when the teams are real
d.caption: Real meaning 12.1's structural reasons — different **permissions**, different **owners**, or a context budget that genuinely does not fit. **A team that exists because the agent list was getting long is 10.1's “this graph is getting long” one level up, and that was the weakest reason to nest anything.** Beyond one level the structure mirrors an org chart, which **imports the cost without the reason**.
